power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: The skills and behaviours underpinning interoperability within the JESIP Joint Doctrine

text.text: In 2012, the Joint Emergency Services Interoperability Principles (JESIP) were established to set a national standard for joint working across emergency services in the UK.
The JESIP Joint Doctrine is the programme's central policy document, setting out the principles and expectations for effective multi-agency working.
However, research has identified a gap between organisational buy-in to these principles and their application in practice.

This study sought to identify the skills and behaviours underpinning interoperability within the JESIP Joint Doctrine and consider how its content might be refined to better support multi-agency working.
A qualitative document analysis of the Joint Doctrine (Version 3.1) was conducted using Braun and Clarke's six-phase approach to thematic analysis.
Three overarching themes were identified: (1) Core Processes Underpinning Interoperability; (2) Key Activities Across the Incident Lifecycle; and (3) Organisational Structures Shaping the Response.
Drawing on these findings, six recommendations were formulated for potential revisions to the doctrine to better support multi-agency operations.

Namely, giving greater prominence to communication and decision-making, clarifying the incident lifecycle, recognising the psychological challenges associated with implementing the doctrine, strengthening opportunities for continuous joint learning, and streamlining the doctrine.

Overall, the findings provide a clearer understanding of how interoperability is represented within the JESIP Joint Doctrine and how its guidance might be refined to better support its application in practice.
Findings also extend beyond the UK emergency services, offering insight to support multi-agency operations in other highstakes organisational domains.
During major emergencies, it is essential that emergency response teams work together cohesively to save lives.
This is known as interoperability.

Emergency teams operate in unconventional, high-stakes environments where failure can have devastating consequences (Bell et al., 2018) and where members face intense physical, psychological, and interpersonal strain (Driskell et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Emergency teams operate in unconventional, high-stakes environments where failure can have devastating consequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bell et al., 2018)</ref> and where members face intense physical, psychological, and interpersonal strain <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Driskell et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Such conditions demand effective multi-team coordination, as sub-teams from across the emergency services must combine their expertise to achieve shared goals (Marks et al., 2001; Power, 2018).
text.formatted: Such conditions demand effective multi-team coordination, as sub-teams from across the emergency services must combine their expertise to achieve shared goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Marks et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Power, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: However, multi-team collaboration introduces additional structural and social challenges, including role confusion, goal conflict, and distrust (Lanaj et al., 2013; Luciano et al., 2021; Power & Alison, 2017a; Power & Alison 2017b; Power et al., 2024).
text.formatted: However, multi-team collaboration introduces additional structural and social challenges, including role confusion, goal conflict, and distrust <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Lanaj et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Luciano et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Power & Alison, 2017a;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Power & Alison 2017b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Power et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The UK Home Office launched the Joint Emergency Services Interoperability Principles (JESIP) in 2012 to support effective multi-team working, but despite continued national investment (Cabinet Office, 2022; Home Office 2023a; 2023b), research has identified a principle-implementation gap for interoperability (Power et al., 2025) where emergency team members are supportive of joint working, but struggle to implement it in practice.
text.formatted: The UK Home Office launched the Joint Emergency Services Interoperability Principles (JESIP) in 2012 to support effective multi-team working, but despite continued national investment (Cabinet Office, 2022; Home Office 2023a; 2023b), research has identified a principle-implementation gap for interoperability <ref type="bibr">(Power et al., 2025)</ref> where emergency team members are supportive of joint working, but struggle to implement it in practice.

text.text: Research has sought to address this gap in several ways.

First, researchers have advocated for greater attention to be paid to the psychological processes involved in multi-agency teamwork (e.g., shared social identity, trust), highlighting that interoperability is a social process and finding that a shared sense of connection between team members is essential for joint working (Davidson et al., 2022; 2023; 2025; Power et al, 2018; 2024; 2025).
text.formatted: First, researchers have advocated for greater attention to be paid to the psychological processes involved in multi-agency teamwork (e.g., shared social identity, trust), highlighting that interoperability is a social process and finding that a shared sense of connection between team members is essential for joint working <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Davidson et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Power et al, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2025)</ref>.

text.text: Second, research has sought to evaluate the strategies used by JESIP to train emergency responders in interoperability.

This has included evaluations of joint training, which have highlighted a need for regular, in-person, face-to-face events (Power et al., 2025) that are immersive and realistic (Brown et al., 2020) and incorporate a wide range of organisations (Waring et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This has included evaluations of joint training, which have highlighted a need for regular, in-person, face-to-face events <ref type="bibr">(Power et al., 2025)</ref> that are immersive and realistic <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Brown et al., 2020)</ref> and incorporate a wide range of organisations <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Waring et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Third, research has looked to more directly evaluate the effectiveness of JESIP on emergency responding since its launch.

For example, Brown et al. (2021) found in their evaluation of a simulated major incident response that the responserecovery phases used by joint emergency teams did not fit the communication structures in a major incident, instead recommending a three-phase incident structure across responseresolve-recovery should be adopted.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Brown et al. (2021)</ref> found in their evaluation of a simulated major incident response that the responserecovery phases used by joint emergency teams did not fit the communication structures in a major incident, instead recommending a three-phase incident structure across responseresolve-recovery should be adopted.

text.text: Related, research has questioned the utility of decision models used to support teamwork during emergencies (e.g., Boulton, 2025; Power & Alison, 2017; Wilkinson et al., 2019; 2022).
text.formatted: Related, research has questioned the utility of decision models used to support teamwork during emergencies (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Boulton, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Power & Alison, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Wilkinson et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2022)</ref>.

text.text: One document which is central to JESIP is its joint doctrine (JESIP, 2024).
text.formatted: One document which is central to JESIP is its joint doctrine <ref type="bibr">(JESIP, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: No research has so far evaluated the joint doctrine to assess its utility as a unifying resource to support joint working.
At 60 pages long, it is a lengthy and detailed document that has arguably bloated across the years during its iterations, currently on version 3.1.

The goal of this research was to independently evaluate the content of the joint doctrine to identify the core skills and behaviours underpinning interoperability, to provide recommendations on how to enhance focus and streamline this document to better support emergency interoperability.
>Method
text.formatted: <head n="3." >Method</head>

text.text: A qualitative document analysis was undertaken to examine the skills and behaviours underpinning interoperability within the JESIP Joint Doctrine: The Interoperability Framework (Version 3.1; Joint Emergency Services Interoperability Principles [JESIP], 2024).
This approach involves the systematic examination and interpretation of documentary material to identify patterns and generate insights relevant to a specific research question (Gross, 2018).
text.formatted: This approach involves the systematic examination and interpretation of documentary material to identify patterns and generate insights relevant to a specific research question <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Gross, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The Joint Doctrine was selected because it provides UK-wide guidance on the actions responders should take during multi-agency incidents of any scale, with the aim of improving interoperability.
The analysis was guided by the following research question: What skills and behaviours underpinning interoperability are outlined within the JESIP Joint Doctrine?
The document was analysed in full using Braun and Clarke's six-phase approach to thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006).
text.formatted: The document was analysed in full using Braun and Clarke's six-phase approach to thematic analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Braun & Clarke, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: In line with this approach, the analysis began with a period of familiarisation involving repeated readings of the document to develop a thorough understanding of its content.
Following this, segments of text relevant to the research question were systematically coded at a semantic level.
Although coding was guided by the study's focus on skills and behaviours, the specific codes and themes were developed inductively.
The resulting codes and associated extracts were then reviewed to identify recurring patterns of meaning and develop candidate themes.
These themes were subsequently reviewed and refined to ensure that they were coherent, distinct, and accurately representative of the data.
After this phase, each theme was defined and named to reflect its content.
Report production involved selecting extracts from each theme to support a coherent account of the findings.
The analysis was conducted by the first author of this report using NVivo 14, with the wider team contributing to theme development and refinement throughout.
Ethical approval was not required because the study involved analysis of a publicly available document and did not involve human participants.
The analysis generated three overarching themes, each comprising several associated subthemes (Figure 1
text.formatted: The analysis generated three overarching themes, each comprising several associated subthemes (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>

text.text: The doctrine outlines several mechanisms for communicating information.

These include "face-to-face" co-location (p. 13), the establishment of "clear lines of communication" (pp. 51, 56-57) supported by "robust… interoperable communications" (p. 13), and the use of standardised tools and frameworks to ensure that information is communicated effectively.

For example, responders are expected to "convey incident information using the M/ETHANE model" (p. 36), and to deliver structured briefings using tools such as the "IIMARCH template" so that decisions and agreed actions are relayed in a way "that can be easily understood by those who will carry out actions or support activities" (p. 31).
The doctrine also emphasises a range of qualities that communications should possess.
These include the use of "language which is clear, and free from technical jargon and abbreviations" (p. 13).

Similarly, responders are expected to use "plain language" (p. 9) and ensure that communications are "concise" (pp. 9, 15, 34), "simple" (p. 34), "reliable and accurate" (p. 14), and "readily understood by all agencies involved" (p. 9).

The importance of communication quality is also reflected in expectations relating to communication with the public, with emergency alerts also expected to be clear, concise and aligned with other communications being issued.
The communication process is further underpinned by expectations relating to the gathering of information and intelligence.

In this context, information refers to "all forms of information obtained, recorded or processed", while intelligence is conceptualised as "information that has been subject to… Evaluation… Risk assessment… [and] Analysis" (p. 25).
text.formatted: In this context, information refers to "all forms of information obtained, recorded or processed", while intelligence is conceptualised as "information that has been subject to… Evaluation… Risk assessment… <ref type="bibr">[and]</ref> Analysis" (p. 25).

text.text: In outlining what should be gathered, the doctrine states that responders should "gather relevant information about the incident" (p. 33) and "identify priorities, resources, capabilities and limitations for an effective response" (p. 12).
Responders are also expected to gather information that may support subsequent recovery.
For example, "recovery issues should be considered as early as possible during the response phase, including the identification of … information that may later inform the recovery phase" (p. 39).
Expectations concerning information sharing appeared to cluster around four broad categories of information: decisions, resources, risks and the situation.

In relation to decisions and resources, for example, responders are expected to share "information from all available sources along with… decisions taken" (p. 14), as well as details regarding "what assets have been, or are being, deployed" (p. 16).

They are also expected to carry out dynamic risk assessments reflecting "the tasks and objectives to be achieved, the hazards identified and the likelihood of harm from those hazards" (p. 27) and share the results with all agencies involved.
In terms of situational information, the doctrine specifies that responders should "freely share what they know" and "make uncertainties and assumptions absolutely clear" (p. 33).
Decision-making is presented in the doctrine as a collaborative and iterative process through which responders develop a shared understanding of an evolving situation and use it
Developing an accurate and shared understanding of the situation is a central component of the decision-making process.
To achieve this, responders are expected to make a "sustained effort to reach a common view" (p. 25) that takes account of "any specific threats, hazards and the risk of harm" (p. 26).
Accordingly, the doctrine stipulates that information should be evaluated and filtered in terms of "relevance", "accuracy", "source reliability", "credibility" and "timeliness" (p. 32-34).
Responders are also expected to "challenge their own understanding" and "the understanding of others" and, where concerns remain, "take steps to update, reconcile and check the information" (pp.
The doctrine outlines a range of strategic, practical and risk-related considerations for evaluating response options.
These include assessing whether a proposed response aligns with "the strategic direction", can be "done with the available resources", and is "legal, morally defensible and justifiable" (p. 28).

The process also involves determining which organisation is best placed "to take the lead role" (p. 15) and whether those assigned to a particular task are appropriately "trained and equipped" (p. 38).

Determining whether agencies share a common understanding of key aspects of the situation, including "potential outcomes", "critical uncertainties", and "key assumptions" (p. 30), represents a further consideration.
Ensuring that any proposed action aligns with the overarching aim of "working together, saving lives [and] reducing harm" is another (p. 30).
text.formatted: Ensuring that any proposed action aligns with the overarching aim of "working together, saving lives <ref type="bibr">[and]</ref> reducing harm" is another (p. 30).

text.text: In addition to developing a shared understanding of the situation and evaluating potential courses of action, responders involved in an incident are expected to reach agreements on various aspects of the response.
These include objectives and priorities, courses of action, roles and responsibilities, as well as communication and co-ordination arrangements.

For example, the doctrine specifies that responders should "jointly agree objectives and a co-ordinated plan to effectively resolve an incident" (p. 14) before prioritising their organisational plans and activities.
They are also expected to "agree appropriate control measures" (p. 12) and ensure that "contingency arrangements… (are) put in place to address reasonably foreseeable events" (p. 28).
Decision-making within the doctrine also encompasses a range of behavioural expectations relating to implementing and reviewing agreed actions.

For example, prior to implementing action, responders are expected to apply "appropriate control measures to ensure any risk is as low as reasonably practicable" (p. 27) and act only once they are "collectively and individually satisfied that the decision controls validate the proposed actions" (p. 29).
The implementation of action, however, is not treated as the endpoint.
Instead, the doctrine conceptualises decision-making as a continuous cycle requiring responders to evaluate, question and update decisions and actions as the situation evolves.
Accordingly, once a course of action has been agreed "it is essential" (p. 29) that the results are fed back into the decision-making process.
The recording of decisions forms another important component of the decision-making process, with a range of associated behavioural expectations outlined throughout the doctrine.

Specifically, it emphasises that decisions should be recorded "in an appropriate way… to prove and justify actions that have been taken" (p. 35), reflecting the potential for decisions made during multi-agency incidents to be subject to later scrutiny.
This emphasis is reinforced by the observation that "legal cases are often focused on the recording of information" (p. 35).

Accordingly, "as an absolute minimum", responders should record "what decision has been made", "the rationale behind this decision, including consideration of other options", the "action required to implement the decision", and the "date and time the decision was made" (p. 35).
The second theme captures the key activities responders are expected to undertake throughout the incident lifecycle.
It encompasses activities relating to early co-location, establishing necessary arrangements, co-ordinating and maintaining the response, and postincident debriefing and learning.
Some of these activities align directly with the five JESIP principles.
Early co-location and co-ordination, for example, are explicitly identified as principles of joint working.
However, the behavioural expectations communicated across the doctrine extend beyond those explicitly outlined within the principles.

These include establishing communication arrangements and shared situational awareness during the early stages of an incident, discussing the available resources and activities of each responder organisation, agreeing priorities, and making joint decisions.

The doctrine also stipulates that maintaining an effective multi-agency response involves carrying out various activities that support both operational activity and shared situational awareness as an incident develops.
Beyond the immediate response, responders are expected to review the response and share learning to inform future responses.
Figure 2 summarises these activities across the incident lifecycle.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">2</ref> summarises these activities across the incident lifecycle.

text.text: The third and final overarching theme captures the organisational structures shaping the response.
It encompasses the actors involved in the response, together with the frameworks and tools that structure how the response is carried out.
Although the doctrine is aimed "at ALL responder organisations across the UK" (p. 6), many of the behavioural expectations it sets out are directed towards particular actors.

These include responders responsible for organising and co-ordinating the response, those responsible for generating, sharing and interpreting information, and those responsible for initiating and implementing operational activity.

Alongside these role-specific expectations, the doctrine specifies a range of frameworks and tools designed to structure and standardise key skills and behaviours underpinning effective joint working.
Consistent with the wider findings, these align closely with the overarching themes of communication, decision-making, and key activities across the incident lifecycle.
Table 1 summarises these organisational structures and provides illustrative examples of the skills and behaviours associated with them.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> summarises these organisational structures and provides illustrative examples of the skills and behaviours associated with them.

text.text: Use structured briefings to communicate decisions and actions (e.g. with the JDM initially and IIMARCH as the incident develops), follow the process for developing a working strategy, and use the strategy to confirm a common view of the situation, potential consequences and required actions.
Note.
The skills and behaviours presented are illustrative examples identified within the doctrine.

A document analysis of the JESIP Joint Doctrine has highlighted several opportunities to streamline its content to improve clarity, comprehension, and practical application across multi-agency groups.

Specifically, we identified three overarching content themes: (1) Core Processes Underpinning Interoperability, (2) Key Activities Across the Incident Lifecycle, and (3) Organisational Structures Shaping the Response.
Drawing on these findings, we provide the following six recommendations for how the doctrine might be revised to better support multiagency operations.
Decision-making and communication are fundamental processes that underpin effective interoperability, cutting across the five JESIP principles and different stages of an incident.
However, these processes are currently distributed throughout the doctrine, rather than being clearly articulated as central mechanisms through which interoperability is achieved.
We recommend giving greater prominence to these processes, highlighting how effective communication and joint decision-making collectively support coordinated multiagency action.
The doctrine outlines a range of activities that support interoperability at different stages of an incident, but the relationships between these activities could be made more explicit.

We recommend presenting a clearer incident lifecycle (e.g., Figure 2) that illustrates how key activities connect, from initial co-location and information sharing through to joint decision-making, coordinated action, and post-incident debriefing and learning.
text.formatted: We recommend presenting a clearer incident lifecycle (e.g., Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">2</ref>) that illustrates how key activities connect, from initial co-location and information sharing through to joint decision-making, coordinated action, and post-incident debriefing and learning.

text.text: Importantly, this should be presented as a continuous cycle, recognising how lessons identified through joint reflection and debriefing should inform future planning, preparedness, and exercising.
This would help practitioners understand how the different elements of the doctrine fit together and reinforce the importance of continuous improvement in interoperability.
Although the doctrine is intended to support multi-agency working, much of its content is oriented towards the structures and responsibilities of the core emergency services.

We recommend reviewing the relevance and accessibility of its content for the wider response community, including organisations with different roles, responsibilities, and levels of familiarity with JESIP.

In particular, it may be helpful to distinguish between the key principles, processes, and behaviours that should directly inform action and the supporting information provided to develop broader knowledge and understanding.
This would help ensure that the doctrine remains relevant and accessible across different organisations and operational contexts.
including the psychological challenges of implementing the doctrine and how these might be addressed through training and exercising

The doctrine provides important structures and processes for supporting interoperability, but their effective implementation depends on how individuals and teams think, communicate, and behave under pressure.

Research highlights that psychological and social factors, including stress, uncertainty, cognitive demands, interpersonal relationships, and organisational identities, can influence the application of interoperability principles in practice (e.g., Davidson et al., 2022; 2023; 2025; Power et al., 2018; 2024; 2025; Waring et al., 2026).

text.text: We recommend giving greater recognition to these challenges and considering how realistic, multi-agency training and exercising can better prepare responders to recognise and manage them.
This would help address the gap between understanding the doctrine and applying it effectively during incidents.

For example, Power et al. (2026) has shown how psychological skills training can have lasting positive impacts on outgroup attitudes between emergency response teams, alongside wider research considering the beneficial role of psychology and non-technical skills for emergency training (e.g., Butler et al., 2020; Davidson et al., 2025).
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Power et al. (2026)</ref> has shown how psychological skills training can have lasting positive impacts on outgroup attitudes between emergency response teams, alongside wider research considering the beneficial role of psychology and non-technical skills for emergency training (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Butler et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Davidson et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Effective interoperability depends not only on how agencies work together during incidents, but also on how they collectively learn and improve over time.
Although the doctrine recognises the importance of joint learning, we recommend positioning this as a continuous process that extends beyond individual incidents and formal debriefing activities.

Greater emphasis could be placed on shared reflection, the identification and dissemination of lessons, and opportunities for agencies to learn together through regular training, exercising, and operational experience.
Importantly, this should involve the wider response community to support the development of shared understanding, relationships, and practices across organisational boundaries.
The doctrine contains a substantial amount of valuable information, but its breadth and detail may make it difficult for readers to identify and retain the most important messages.

We recommend reviewing the overall structure to reduce duplication, consolidate related content, and establish a clearer hierarchy between core principles, practical guidance, and supporting information.
Organising the doctrine around the central processes, key activities, and organisational structures identified through this analysis may provide a more intuitive framework.
The aim should be to retain the substance of the doctrine while making its central messages easier to understand, remember, and apply in practice.
The JESIP Joint Doctrine provides an important foundation for supporting interoperability across the emergency response community.
Our analysis has identified opportunities to strengthen its clarity, accessibility, and practical application.

Central to these recommendations is the need to provide a more coherent account of the processes, activities, and organisational structures that underpin effective multi-agency working, while recognising the human and psychological challenges of putting these into practice.

Taken together, these recommendations are intended to support a more streamlined and accessible doctrine that clearly communicates the core principles of interoperability, their application across the incident lifecycle, the psychological impact of implementing principles under pressure, and the importance of continuous joint learning.

Rather than fundamentally changing the doctrine, the aim is to strengthen its existing foundations and ensure that it provides clear, relevant, and actionable guidance for the wider response community.
Further, the recommendations outlined have relevance beyond the emergency response community, providing guidelines for any high-risk industry seeking to support multi-agency operations.
Ultimately, these revisions could help bridge the gap between understanding the principles of interoperability and applying them effectively in practice.
